domain: Safety Engineering / Organizational Learning / High-Reliability Organizations
topic_summary: Analysis of how aviation and nuclear industries retain catastrophe-avoidance competence across decades without recurring real catastrophes. The kernel contest examines whether simulation-based training constitutes genuine exercise of safety competence or whether only actual catastrophic events can maintain the organizational knowledge required for prevention.

key_entities: Aviation industry (commercial flight operations with simulator-based training)
Nuclear power industry (reactor operations with emergency drill protocols)
Regulatory bodies (FAA, NRC - mandate recurrent training)
Organizational memory systems (incident databases, training curricula)
key_tensions: Simulation fidelity vs real-world unpredictability (can drills capture true catastrophe dynamics)
Competence decay vs training frequency (how often must skills be exercised to remain viable)
key_mechanisms: Recurrent simulator training (mandated periodic exposure to emergency scenarios)
Incident investigation and knowledge codification (NTSB/NRC reports feeding training updates)
Regulatory enforcement of training standards (license renewal contingent on demonstrated competence)
key_absences: Absence of discussion of near-miss incidents as intermediate validation points between simulation and catastrophe
Absence of analysis of industries that lost catastrophe-avoidance competence (e.g., offshore drilling, chemical plants with long incident-free periods preceding major failures)

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The shared commitment that catastrophe-avoidance competence must be actively maintained through repeated exercise, not merely documented in procedures
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Regulatory bodies (FAA, NRC) ground legitimacy in demonstrated performance under test conditions; industry grounds legitimacy in zero-catastrophe operational records

readings.commitment: High-fidelity simulation constitutes genuine exercise of catastrophe-avoidance competence; the cognitive and procedural demands are structurally equivalent to real events
readings.authority_grounding: Regulatory validation through zero-catastrophe outcomes in industries with mature simulator programs; transfer-of-training research showing skill retention
readings.expected_structural_delta: Training infrastructure becomes the primary competence-maintenance mechanism; real catastrophes are prevented rather than experienced; competence is measured by simulator performance metrics

readings.commitment: Only actual catastrophic events provide the organizational learning and visceral stakes required to maintain genuine competence; simulation is rehearsal but not the real thing
readings.authority_grounding: Historical pattern of competence decay in long-incident-free periods (normalization of deviance); distinction between knowing-about and knowing-how under true stakes
readings.expected_structural_delta: Competence decays invisibly during incident-free periods; organizations become vulnerable precisely when they appear safest; simulation creates false confidence; real catastrophes are necessary system resets

readings.commitment: Near-miss incidents and minor failures provide sufficient real-world feedback to validate and update simulator training without requiring full catastrophes
readings.authority_grounding: Safety science literature on precursor events; organizational learning theory emphasizing weak signals; incident reporting systems as competence-maintenance infrastructure
readings.expected_structural_delta: Competence maintenance requires hybrid system: simulators for routine skill preservation plus active near-miss investigation and integration; catastrophes are neither necessary nor sufficient alone
